prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its actions, which made possible incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six opening ballots put GLP-1 first, but I do not rest the case on that agreement. On the merits, it is an unusually complete path from hormone physiology to medicine. Holst showed the physiology and secretion of the active GLP-1 forms in humans, Drucker defined GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology and receptor signalling, and Mojsov identified and synthesised the active peptide. Large independent randomized trials now show benefit in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular disease and kidney disease, so the work is mature and not premature. The three-person trio is the most defensible one, because it rewards the discovery of the mechanism and keeps the prize centred on physiology.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The Mojsov versus Habener priority question on the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is not resolved by the supplied text. A basic-science trio leaves out Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, whose liraglutide and semaglutide work produced the drugs that actually changed practice, and the prize could be read as honouring the hormone while omitting the medicine. The three-person cap forces this exclusion, and I accept that it is a real cost.

responses.point: Marie ranks GLP-1 first but puts TNF blockade (Feldmann and Maini) second as a clean two-person, fully mature story, ahead of CAR-T.
responses.response: I agree that B051 is mature, well attributed and clinically important, and I do not dismiss it as merely therapeutic. My reservation is that it rests on a concept, TNF as the dominant driver of synovial inflammation, whose underlying biology involves earlier contributors who are not in the credited names. That makes the discovery narrative less self-contained than GLP-1 or CAR-T. Only one member ranked it in the top three, so I would not make it the second part of a shared prize at this stage.

responses.point: Thomas favours the three basic-science GLP-1 contributors (Holst, Drucker, Mojsov), accepts that the allocation is contested, and treats Knudsen's industrial work as secondary.
responses.response: I agree with the trio, but I would not leave Knudsen out lightly, because the recognition is only complete if the translational step is acknowledged somewhere. If the committee wants to honour drug development, the three-person cap means someone from the basic trio would have to be dropped, and I would not want that. The citation should therefore state that it rewards the physiology and its pharmacology, and the Knudsen question should be recorded as a deliberate choice.

responses.point: Abdel places optogenetics third behind CAR-T, backs Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann, and acknowledges that six credited names cannot fit into three.
responses.response: I rank B007 third as well, but there is a point I want us to be honest about. It is a research tool, and it has not yet delivered a medical therapy beyond early retinal work. The three-person limit also forces us to exclude Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck, and that exclusion cannot be defended on priority alone. I would hold B007 as an alternative, not as the preferred configuration. If it goes forward, the committee has to say explicitly why the tool counts under Physiology or Medicine and why these three were chosen.

responses.point: Sten ranks BCR-ABL inhibition (Druker, Sawyers, Lydon) second, above CAR-T, as a fully confirmed targeted-therapy paradigm that may be overdue.
responses.response: I take this seriously, since imatinib is a landmark case of rational drug design. It was ranked first by no one and top three by only one member. My concern, which you also raise, is that it reads as an application of oncogene and kinase biology that others discovered earlier. That weakens its claim as a distinct discovery compared with CAR-T, which created a new modality. I would keep B032 on the shortlist for discussion, but I would not move it above B026 on the strength of the evidence presented.

responses.point: Rickard places CAR-T second, crediting June and Sadelain with the core invention, and unfolded protein response (Mori, Walter) third as a clean fundamental discovery.
responses.response: I agree that the CAR-T core is best credited to June and Sadelain, and the shortlist entry also lists Rosenberg. I would keep Rosenberg out of any CAR-T configuration, because his adoptive cell therapy and TIL work is a separate line. I part ways with the UPR ranking: it is conceptually elegant, but its medical consequences are mostly indirect, and only one member put it in the top three. For this year it ranks below B026 and B007.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to reward discovery of the mechanism, drug development, or both, and whether Knudsen should displace one of the basic trio.
Resolution of the Mojsov versus Habener priority question on the active GLP-1 peptide.
Whether a second, distinct achievement such as CAR-T should share the prize, which would force a reduction in the GLP-1 trio because of the three-person cap.
My knowledge of detailed priority histories comes from memory and is not verified against the supplied nominations.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the GLP-1 candidates. Per my profile, I overlap with Thomas Perlmann as a frequent co-author on dopamine neuron topics, and I worked with Paul Greengard as a postdoctoral fellow. Neither connection bears on B033 or the alternatives B026 and B007. This is a documented connection and not a disqualifying one.
